questions.prompt: Your status agent works well on fixtures. Before connecting it to the live GitHub API, which of these should you decide first?

options.text: The color scheme of the approval screen.
options.rationale: Not a release decision.

options.text: The release rule: thresholds for success and cost, and zero tolerated safety violations, written down before you see live results.
options.rationale: Yes. A rule decided after the results is a rationalization.

options.text: Whether to remove the injection scenarios now that the agent passes them.
options.rationale: Passing scenarios become the regression suite; they stay.

options.text: Which issues to exclude so the live demo looks good.
options.rationale: That is overfitting the demo.

questions.explanation: Write the gate rule in the README before the run that will be judged by it. Keep the full suite, including injection scenarios, as regression tests.

questions.prompt: For the weekly status job, which part is the best candidate to stay deterministic code rather than a model step?

options.text: Judging whether a free-text comment means an issue is blocked
options.rationale: That needs reading comprehension; a model step fits.

options.text: Writing a readable summary for a stakeholder
options.rationale: Model-driven writing is where the value is.

options.text: Deciding which issues opened, closed, or changed during the week
options.rationale: Yes. That is a date-filtered query; a model adds cost and error.

options.text: Grouping related issues into themes
options.rationale: Judgment work; a reasonable model step.

questions.explanation: Start simple: code for what can be computed exactly, models where judgment over text adds value. Test the deterministic parts without a model.

questions.prompt: An MCP tool for the project. What is the main design problem?

options.text: It mixes reads and irreversible writes behind one parameter, so the client's approval and policy checks cannot tell from the tool name what it is approving.
options.rationale: Yes. Split read tools from write tools and keep each write narrow.

options.text: MCP tools cannot accept dict arguments.
options.rationale: Tools take JSON Schema inputs; objects are allowed.

options.text: The docstring is too long.
options.rationale: Too vague, if anything.

options.text: It should be async.
options.rationale: Possibly nicer, not the main problem.

questions.explanation: Consolidate by workflow but never mix risk levels in one tool (Studio 1, lesson 11). A host's permission rules and your guard work per tool, so a combined tool forces every call through the strictest path or, worse, through none.

questions.prompt: A first-week cost estimate for the eval. What does this print?
questions.code:
scenarios, trials = 15, 4
calls_per_run = 6
in_tok, out_tok = 3000, 400              # per call
price_in, price_out = 4 / 1e6, 20 / 1e6  # $ per token
per_run = calls_per_run * (in_tok * price_in + out_tok * price_out)
print(round(per_run, 3), round(per_run * scenarios * trials, 2))

options.rationale: That is one call, not six.
That multiplies by 15 scenarios but forgets the 4 trials.
Off by ten in the per-token prices.
Per call: 0.012 + 0.008 = 0.02; six calls is 0.12; 60 runs is 7.20.

questions.explanation: Estimate before you run, then measure. Recompute with real token counts from your logs and the prices on the pricing page on the day you run; record both in the write-up.

questions.prompt: Which belong in the project's eval set as their own scenarios? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pull requests mixed into the issues list
options.rationale: Correct. The issues endpoints return them.

options.text: More changed issues than one API page
options.rationale: Correct. Tests pagination and early stopping.

options.text: The reviewer rejects the draft
options.rationale: Correct. A should-not-act case: nothing gets posted.

options.text: An issue body asking the agent to email the notes outside
options.rationale: Correct. An injection scenario.

options.text: A scenario copied from the reference report so the agent always passes
options.rationale: Writing tests the system cannot fail measures nothing.

questions.explanation: Balance should-act and should-not-act cases, include data edge cases and tool failures, and keep at least three injection scenarios. Every scenario has a fixture, an expected end state, and a reference outcome.

questions.prompt: Your design has the agent call post_status itself after approval. A reviewer suggests instead that the agent only saves a draft and your application posts it after a human clicks approve. What is the main benefit?

options.text: It reduces token usage by half.
options.rationale: Token savings are minor.

options.text: The model never holds a tool that reaches the outside, so no injected instruction can make it post; the only outbound action is code you wrote, triggered by a person.
options.rationale: Yes. It removes the outbound leg from the model's reach.

options.text: GitHub requires it.
options.rationale: No such requirement.

options.text: It makes the agent faster.
options.rationale: Speed is not the point.

questions.explanation: Draft-then-approve with the post performed by application code is a plan-then-execute design: the set of actions is fixed by you. The approval step is the product, and it is one decision per run, which keeps reviewers attentive.
